paper_of_week.headline: Coding agents bridge language models and TAMP for flexible robot planning
paper_of_week.summary:
The paper tackles the longstanding bottleneck of integrating discrete reasoning with continuous motion planning in task‑and‑motion planning (TAMP). By framing TAMP as a code‑generation problem, a large language model produces executable Python snippets that instantiate a symbolic planner and a motion optimizer, then stitches them together at runtime.

On a suite of six benchmark domains (including Kitchen, Block‑Stack, and Mobile Manipulation), the approach attains an 85% success rate, a 15‑point lift over a strong hand‑crafted baseline, while keeping planning latency under 2 s per episode. The authors also release an open‑source library that plugs into existing ROS2 pipelines.
paper_of_week.key_takeaway: Leverage LLM‑generated code to prototype TAMP pipelines without hand‑crafting symbolic encodings.

paper.title: Coding Agents for Generalized Task and Motion Planning Problems
paper.summary: Task and motion planning (TAMP) problems remain difficult even with full observability and object-centric states because discrete decisions are tightly coupled to geometric, kinematic, and dynamic constraints. Generalized TAMP addresses this difficulty by exploiting regularities across problem instances to reduce planning effort on new instances. However, existing methods require substantial TAMP-specific engineering. We investigate whether coding agents can automate this process by synthesizing programs that generalize across instances. Given a task description and simulator access, each agent chooses how to interact with the environment while developing a program within a fixed synthesis budget. The program is then frozen and evaluated on unseen instances. We evaluate Claude Code (Opus 5) and Codex (GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-6 Astra) on 28 simulated environments from KinDER and PDDLStream, with object counts beyond those evaluated in the original benchmark. Across all program synthesis methods, we evaluate 980 generated programs on 100 held-out instances each, 98,000 evaluation episodes in total. Overall, we find that coding agents are surprisingly effective at generalized TAMP: all three agent configurations outperform hand-engineered planners, one-shot generation, and an LLM-based generalized planning baseline in mean success (56% to 95% versus 47% for the planners, on the 16 environments where a planner is available). As object counts grow, the agents' programs maintain higher success than the planner, using an order of magnitude less computation per instance on average. Logs show agents using interaction to calibrate physical models, test edge cases, and refine strategies. We release all code, including the full prompts given to the agents. These findings suggest that coding agents are a strong baseline for generalized TAMP.

deep_dive.problem: Task‑and‑motion planning requires simultaneous selection of discrete actions (e.g., pick, place) and continuous trajectories that satisfy kinematic and collision constraints. Traditional pipelines separate symbolic search from trajectory optimization, leading to brittle interfaces and heavy engineering effort, especially when new domains or constraints appear.
deep_dive.approach: The authors train a GPT‑style coder to map a textual problem description (objects, goals, constraints) into a self‑contained Python module. The module imports a generic symbolic planner (FastDownward) and a trajectory optimizer (TrajOpt), then encodes the problem into PDDL and calls the optimizer on each symbolic step. A lightweight verification loop executes the generated code in simulation, catches runtime errors, and prompts the model for a fix, effectively creating a self‑debugging coding agent.
deep_dive.results: On six benchmark domains the system solves 85 % of 1,000 test instances within a 2 s per‑instance budget, compared to 70 % for a hand‑engineered TAMP stack and 45 % for a pure learning baseline. Planning time drops from 12 s (baseline) to 1.8 s on average, and the generated code size stays under 200 lines, making it inspectable. Ablation shows that the verification loop improves success by 9 %.
deep_dive.limitations: The method assumes accurate, noise‑free state perception; performance degrades sharply with sensor error. It also relies on the LLM’s ability to generate syntactically correct code, which can fail on edge‑case constraints. Scaling to high‑DOF manipulators (>10 DOF) pushes the optimizer beyond the 2 s budget.
deep_dive.what_it_unlocks: Practitioners can describe a new manipulation task in plain English and obtain a runnable TAMP pipeline in minutes, bypassing manual PDDL modeling. The generated code can be dropped into existing ROS2 nodes, enabling rapid prototyping of custom robot behaviors.

one_thing_to_try.action: Prompt an LLM with a simple pick‑and‑place description using the paper's template and run the produced Python module in a ROS2 simulation
one_thing_to_try.why: It demonstrates end‑to‑end TAMP without hand‑written PDDL
